newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OLYMPICS-IOC PLAN TOUGHER RULES TO STOP JUNK COMMERCIALISM.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC PLAN TOUGHER RULES TO STOP JUNK COMMERCIALISM.

text.p: Olympic chiefs plan to tighten their rules on commercialism after the controversial Atlanta Games to stop the world's most prestigious sporting event being degraded by street vendors selling junk memorabilia.
Atlanta was heavily criticised for commercial excesses. Some said the large number of city-backed private vendors allowed to clog the city centre had made the Games look like a huge flea market.
International Olympic Committee (IOC) officials said on Wednesday they were worried that some products could damage the image of the Games and there would be tougher rules in the future.

"We learn from every Olympic experience," IOC vice-president Dick Pound said. "By recent experience we will take a look at the host city contract to deal with the ability of a host city to ambush the Olympic organising committee.
"Frankly it had not occurred to us that a city would do that."
IOC marketing director Michael Payne added: "There was not quite a commemorative Olympic toilet seat cover (in Atlanta) but it got pretty close. Some of the products we vetoed."

The IOC has a number of official sponsors and rules about how the Olympics Games can be used in advertising. Pound said the IOC would not give the Games to cities in the future unless it agreed with their commercial plans.

The IOC cannot write any new rules into binding legal contracts until the 2004 Summer Olympics since the deals with cities due to host Winter and Summer Games in the next six years have already been signed.

Sydney is hosting the next Summer Games in the year 2000 while Nagano in Japan and Salt Lake City in the United States are staging the next two Winter Games in 1998 and 2002 respectively. The venue for the 2004 Summer Games has yet to be decided.
But Pound said: "Officials from the 1998, 2000 and 2002 Games were in Atlanta and saw what could go wrong. They are enthusiastic about not getting into the same situation."

The IOC is still waiting to carry out a full Atlanta post-mortem and was unable to discuss the Games in detail at Wednesday's executive board meeting because all the reports on the organisation were not complete.

IOC director general Francois Carrard, however, denied a media report that the Games had lost money. The body has yet to receive a detailed financial report which is unlikely to be ready until the end of the year at the earliest.
"There are no figures on the table, under the table or in the drawers," he said. "We have not had a final account yet. There is talk of a modest profit but there is no talk of a deficit."
U.S. Olympic Committee official (USOC) John Krimsky added: "I'm expecting good news, maybe not great news. But good news for me is anything black."

The Atlanta Games were funded largely through the private sector, which is unusual. The IOC expressed concern afterwards that they did not have the backing from the state which gave previous Olympics an important safety net.

It came under heavy fire from the media around the world for being badly organised. The IOC is looking into criticisms about transport, accommodation and technology in addition to those of commercial excesses.
